text.title: Two-Pass: Free-Form Reasoning Then Structured Extraction Core Rules
text.summary: Run hard reasoning in free text on the strong model, then extract into the strict schema with a cheap model. 7 testable rules grounding the two-pass-reason-then-extract methodology. Each rule pairs a binary check + sourced rationale. Corrected 2026-08-04: the accuracy loss this methodology recovers is caused by the FORMAT INSTRUCTION in the prompt, not by the decoder's grammar mask — see the correction section at the end.

section.title: Background
section.p: For tasks where reasoning quality matters more than output format, never lock the reasoning step into strict structured output. Split the work into two passes: pass 1 produces free-form reasoning on the strong model, pass 2 extracts the structured answer with a cheap model.

Cost trade-offs: when two-pass beats single-pass and how to size the extraction prompt. Two-pass adds a second model call but the extractor is small (Haiku class) and its prompt is short. The strong-model output stays roughly the same length whether wrapped in strict JSON or not, so the marginal cost of pass 2 is the extractor's input/output tokens — a small fraction of the strong-model bill.

rule.statement: Tasks combining deep reasoning + strict schema MUST split into two passes: strong model answering in free text (or extended thinking) with NO format instruction in its prompt, then cheap model with strict structured output over the strong-model transcript.

rationale.source: arXiv:2604.03616, The Format Tax, Lee / D'Antoni / Berg-Kirkpatrick (UC San Diego), 2026-04-04

rule.rationale: The decoupled two-pass shape recovers +6.8 pp on average, improving 42 of 72 model x task x format combinations, measured over MATH-500, GPQA-Diamond, ZebraLogic and WritingBench across 6 open-weight models and 4 closed APIs. Open-weight models lose -3.9 pp on average from the format request alone and -5.8 pp averaged across formats. Frontier closed models have largely absorbed the tax — Claude Haiku, Grok and GPT-5.4-nano show near-zero or positive deltas — so run the A/B before adopting rather than assuming the gain (see ab-vs-single-pass).

rule.statement: Pass 1 MUST NOT use `tool_choice` / `response_format=json_schema` / `output_config.format` / strict grammar constraints — AND its prompt MUST NOT describe the output format, show the schema, or ask for JSON. Dropping the decoder constraint while leaving "reply as JSON matching this schema" in the prompt keeps almost the whole cost. Extended thinking is allowed and encouraged when task difficulty justifies it.
rule.rationale: 92% of statistically significant degradations (McNemar test) are already present with the format-requesting INSTRUCTION alone, before any decoder constraint is applied; the grammar adds little further harm. The mechanism the authors propose is that a format instruction compresses the visible reasoning channel before the model has finished solving, so it commits early. This corrects the earlier rationale in this methodology, which attributed the loss to the grammar mask: the mask was the visible mechanism, the instruction is the cause. Removing the instruction is what recovers accuracy.

rule.statement: Pass 2 MUST use strict structured output (`response_format=json_schema` / `tool_choice` / Pydantic `parse`). Temperature ≤ 0.2.

rationale.source: Anthropic tool-use docs; OpenAI structured outputs docs; arXiv:2604.25359, 2026-04-28

rule.rationale: Extraction is mechanical; determinism is the contract the consumer relies on. Note the residual risk moves rather than disappearing: across 21 models schema compliance is near-perfect while exact leaf-value accuracy is 83.0% on plain text, so pass 2 can be perfectly valid and still carry a wrong value. Spend eval budget on the values, not on compliance.

rule.statement: The strong-model transcript passed to the extractor MUST be capped (e.g. 8K tokens). If reasoning exceeds the cap, summarize first or split the task.
rule.rationale: Long transcripts inflate extractor cost and erode the savings; bounded transcripts keep the 2-pass cost ratio favourable.

rule.statement: Before deploying two-pass, run an A/B vs single-pass on ≥50 representative tasks. Adopt only when accuracy delta ≥ 5% absolute and cost delta ≤ 2x.
rule.rationale: Two-pass is an investment; A/B keeps the decision data-driven and prevents cargo-culting on tasks where single-pass is fine.

rule.statement: When a task requires deep reasoning AND a strict schema, run the strong model in free-text or extended-thinking mode for the reasoning step, then run a cheap extractor model with strict structured output to fill the schema from the strong model's transcript.
rule.rationale: Corrected 2026-08-04. The cost is the FORMAT INSTRUCTION in the prompt, not the grammar mask: The Format Tax (arXiv:2604.03616, 2026-04-04) separates the format request from the constrained decode and finds 92 percent of statistically significant degradations already present with the instruction alone, before any decoder constraint. A format instruction compresses the visible reasoning channel before the model has finished solving, so it commits early. Two-pass restores accuracy — +6.8 pp on average, improving 42 of 72 model x task x format combinations — because pass 1 sees no format request at all, and the extraction step is easy enough that a small model meets the spec at a fraction of the cost. Earlier SLOT / vendor-guide figures of 10–15 percent describe the combined effect and do not isolate the cause.

rule.statement: Use two-pass when (a) the task is reasoning-heavy AND (b) extraction-only accuracy on the cheap model exceeds 95 percent on a held-out sample. If extraction quality is below that threshold, either thicken the schema descriptions or fall back to single-pass on the strong model with an embedded scratchpad.
rule.rationale: Reasoning improvement on the strong model dominates the bill. The extractor is cheap enough that its only constraint is correctness; if a Haiku-class model meets 95+ percent on extraction-only inputs, the savings from preserving the strong model's accuracy justify the second call.

section.title: Correction — 2026-08-04
section.statement: Versions up to 1.1.0 of this methodology attributed the accuracy loss to the grammar mask of strict structured output, citing SLOT (arXiv:2505.04016) and a 2026 vendor guide for a 10-15% drop. The two-pass PRESCRIPTION was right and is unchanged; the CAUSAL story was wrong. The Format Tax (arXiv:2604.03616, 2026-04-04) separates the format-requesting instruction from the grammar-constrained decode and measures each: 92% of significant degradations are present with the instruction alone. Three consequences. First, the fix is to remove the format instruction from the reasoning prompt, not merely to disable constrained decoding — a common half-measure that keeps the cost. Second, a strict schema is NOT a plausible cause of a MISSING required field: under real constrained decoding the grammar makes the closing brace unreachable until every required key is emitted, so an observed ~30% required-field omission rate (Anthropic Agent SDK with `output_format=json_schema` on Sonnet 4.5, internal, production fix was plain text parsed into Pydantic) is evidence that the path was not applying grammar constraints at all — a client integration defect, not the format tax. Third, that production choice — prose then parse — is the researched-correct shape, a degenerate one-pass form of the decoupled two-pass recommended here, not a superstitious workaround. Do not generalise it into "provider structured output is unreliable": those are different code paths and the API path must be measured on its own.

Retained but reframed: the extended-thinking variant (hidden scratchpad, then format) recovers +9.2 pp on average but worsens 15% of combinations (arXiv:2604.03616) — higher mean, higher variance than the two-pass split. Prefer two-pass when a regression on any single task class is unacceptable.

list.item: Latency budget under one second total — two calls cannot fit.
Schema is so simple (single enum, single number) that the strong model's accuracy gap with strict mode is negligible.
Extractor accuracy on extraction-only is below 95 percent — fix that first or stay single-pass.
Task volume is so high that the extra call cost dominates — measure end-to-end before optimising.
